lessons.title: The Nature and Purpose of Marriage
lessons.description: Religious teachings on the purpose of marriage, family roles, cohabitation and arranged marriage.
lessons.content_html:
Marriage Across Religions and Cultures

Marriage is recognised in every major world religion and most human cultures as a significant moral and social institution. While the specific ceremonies, requirements and purposes differ, virtually all traditions treat marriage as more than a legal contract — it is a commitment with spiritual, social and ethical dimensions. This lesson explores how Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism understand marriage, alongside non-religious perspectives on committed relationships.

Key Fact

The concept of cohabitation — couples living together outside marriage — is growing in modern Britain. Religious responses to this range from strong opposition (Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, many Muslim scholars) to greater acceptance in some liberal and non-religious perspectives. Understanding this diversity is essential for the evaluation questions on relationships.

Christianity

Christianity generally regards marriage as a sacred institution created by God. Mark 10:6–8 records Jesus quoting the creation account: “At the beginning of creation God ‘made them male and female’. For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” This teaching presents marriage as a divine design for companionship, mutual support and the bringing up of children.

The Church of England General Synod has described marriage as a gift of God in creation, a lifelong commitment between a man and a woman. Catholic teaching, expressed in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (2360–2363), holds that marriage is a sacrament — one of the seven outward signs of God’s grace — and that its two purposes are the good of the spouses (bonum coniugum) and the procreation and education of children. For Catholics, marriage is indissoluble: once validly made and consummated, it cannot be dissolved. Some Protestant traditions have a more flexible view, particularly on divorce, but all regard marriage as a serious, public commitment before God and community.

On marriage outside the religious tradition, most Christian denominations prefer that members marry other Christians but do not uniformly prohibit interfaith marriages. The Church of England will typically marry couples where one partner is not baptised, with pastoral discretion.

Judaism

In Judaism, marriage (kiddushin, meaning “sanctification”) is a fundamental institution of Jewish life. The ceremony includes the signing of the ketubah, a marriage document setting out the husband’s duties to his wife in matters of support and intimacy. The wedding ceremony culminates in the recitation of the seven blessings (Sheva Berachot), which praise God and invoke blessing on the couple. Marriage is seen as the divinely ordained context for companionship, family and the continuation of the Jewish people. Most denominations discourage but do not absolutely prohibit marriage to non-Jews; intermarriage is a subject of significant communal debate across Orthodox and Progressive communities.

Islam

Islam views marriage (nikah) as a solemn contract (aqd) and a strong religious duty. The Qur’an (30:21) describes marriage as a sign of God’s mercy: He created spouses so that you may find peace in one another, and He has placed between you love and mercy. This verse is central to the Islamic understanding of marriage as an act of worship and a source of tranquillity. The marriage contract requires the free consent of both parties, the presence of witnesses, and the payment of a mahr (dowry) from the groom to the bride as a gift she owns absolutely.

Arranged marriage (more accurately described as assisted marriage) is common in many Muslim communities. Families introduce compatible partners, but the consent of both bride and groom is an Islamic requirement. Forced marriage is explicitly condemned in Islamic teaching as invalid. In Britain, registry office legal ceremonies are typically combined with the religious nikah ceremony.

In Hinduism, marriage is one of the sixteen samskaras (sacred rites of passage) and marks entry into the grihastha (householder) stage of life — the second of the four ashramas. The householder stage is often described as the foundation of the other three stages, because it sustains families, community and religious life. Rama and Sita from the Ramayana are the ideal role models for a married couple: Rama embodies duty, honour and devotion; Sita represents loyalty, virtue and self-sacrifice. Arranged marriage (vivah) is traditional in many Hindu communities, though younger Hindus in Britain increasingly choose their own partners while maintaining family involvement. Interfaith marriage may create tension over which rituals to follow and how to raise children, but views across the British Hindu community are varied.

Sikhism

The Sikh wedding ceremony is called the Anand Karaj (“blissful union”). The couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib four times as the four lavans (wedding hymns from GGS 773–774) are sung, each circuit deepening the couple’s commitment to God and to each other. The ceremony emphasises that the spiritual journey of marriage is undertaken in the presence of and guided by the scripture. Sikhism understands marriage not merely as a social contract but as a merging of two souls on a shared spiritual path. Arranged and assisted marriages are common in Sikh communities.

Buddhism

Buddhism does not treat marriage as a religious sacrament — it is primarily a civil and social matter. The Buddha did not prescribe a specific marriage ceremony in the Pali Canon. However, the Sigalovada Sutta outlines the mutual duties of husband and wife: a husband should be faithful, respectful, loving and provide well; a wife should manage the household well, care for guests, be faithful and protect the family’s wealth. These five mutual duties form the Buddhist ethical framework for married life rather than a ritual requirement. Divorce is not prohibited in Buddhism, though the dhamma (teaching) encourages compassion and the reduction of suffering in all relationships.

Key Fact

The Qur’an (30:21) teaches that God placed love and mercy between married spouses so that partners might find peace in one another. This verse grounds Islamic marriage in divine design rather than social convention alone, making marriage an act of worship and a reflection of God’s mercy.

Non-Religious Perspectives

For Humanists and secular thinkers, marriage is a meaningful public commitment between partners based on love, mutual respect and equality — but its significance comes from the people making the commitment, not from divine sanction. Humanist weddings (legally recognised in Scotland since 2005 and Northern Ireland since 2018, but in England and Wales couples must still have a separate civil ceremony for legal recognition — a Government consultation began in 2025) celebrate the couple’s values and story without religious content. Humanists typically support the right of individuals to choose their relationship structure, including cohabitation, civil partnership or marriage, without moral judgement. British counselling charities (including organisations such as Marriage Care in Britain, a Catholic-founded charity supporting couples and families of all faiths and none) provide relationship support irrespective of religious background.

Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, which came into force in March 2014. Religious responses vary significantly: the Church of England and Roman Catholic Church do not conduct same-sex marriages, though the Church of England has introduced prayers of blessing for same-sex couples. Some liberal Jewish denominations, including many Reform and Progressive synagogues, conduct same-sex weddings. Most Muslim scholars oppose same-sex marriage on the basis of Qur’anic teaching. Some Sikh gurdwaras and some Buddhist communities are more accepting. When answering evaluation questions on this topic, present these as legitimate disagreements between communities rather than advocating for one position.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Marriage questions often ask you to “explain the nature and purpose” or to “explain two similar or different ways” two traditions approach marriage. Make sure you explain both the what (what does the ceremony or contract involve?) and the why (what does this reveal about what marriage means in this tradition?). The Anand Karaj walking around the Guru Granth Sahib four times is a good example: explaining what happens gains description marks, but explaining that each circuit deepens the couple’s spiritual commitment demonstrates understanding. Always link ceremony to belief.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christianity treats marriage as a sacred lifelong commitment; Catholic teaching (CCC 2360–2363) calls it a sacrament; the Church of England describes it as a gift of God. Both ground marriage in Mark 10:6–8.
  • Judaism marks marriage with the ketubah and seven blessings; Islam uses the nikah contract with mahr and requires the free consent of both parties; Sikhism celebrates the Anand Karaj by walking around the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Buddhism views marriage primarily as a civil commitment, using the Sigalovada Sutta’s five mutual duties as the ethical framework; Humanists regard marriage as a meaningful public commitment whose value comes from the partners, not divine sanction.

[2 marks]

Mastering: Two genuinely contrasting views (e.g. Catholic opposition grounded in CCC and the view that sexual intimacy belongs within the sacrament of marriage, vs. a Buddhist or non-religious acceptance that committed cohabitation can be as ethically valid as formal marriage). Both developed with sources; contrast clearly drawn.
Secure: Two contrasting views developed, contrast noted.
Developing: Two views without genuine contrast.
Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Marriage should be for life, whatever the circumstances.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Catholic Christianity: marriage is a sacrament and is indissoluble (CCC 2360–2363); divorce is not recognised.
• Sikhism: the Anand Karaj makes marriage a lifelong spiritual union in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.
• Islam: Qur'an 30:21 presents marriage as God's design for peace and mercy; family stability is a high value.

Arguments against:
• Many Protestant and some Jewish traditions permit divorce in cases of adultery, abuse or irretrievable breakdown.
• Buddhism does not prohibit divorce; reducing suffering (avoiding dukkha) may justify ending an unhappy marriage.
• Humanists argue that a relationship's value lies in its quality, not its legal permanence; forcing people to remain in harmful marriages causes harm.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced evaluation; multiple traditions engaged; non-religious view included; clear justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with references; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument; limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

lessons.title: Sexual Ethics and Contraception
lessons.description: Religious teachings on sex outside marriage, Natural Law, contraception, and divorce across faiths.
lessons.content_html:
Sexual Ethics Across Traditions

Sexual ethics is one of the areas where religious traditions show the greatest internal diversity — from strong absolute positions rooted in natural law or scripture, to more flexible approaches that weigh pastoral context and the well-being of individuals. This lesson examines what each tradition teaches about the purposes of sex, the use of contraception, and attitudes towards divorce, presenting these as legitimate disagreements between and within traditions rather than matters with a single correct answer.

Christianity — Natural Law and the Purpose of Sex

Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) developed the theory of Natural Law, arguing that God has built purposes into human nature that can be discerned by reason. Aquinas identified five primary precepts — fundamental human goods — the second of which is reproduction. From this, Aquinas argued that sexual acts must be open to the possibility of new life in order to be morally permissible. Any sexual act that by its nature cannot result in procreation (for example, contraceptive sex) violates natural law in this approach. This absolutist position has been enormously influential in Catholic moral theology.

The Catholic Church’s position on contraception is set out in the encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968), issued by Pope Paul VI. The encyclical taught that each act of sexual intercourse must remain open to the transmission of life, and that artificial contraception breaks the God-given link between the unitive and procreative dimensions of sex. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2362–2363) affirms that sexual love within marriage is good and holy, united with fruitfulness. Natural family planning (tracking fertility cycles) is permitted as it works with rather than against the body’s natural processes.

The Church of England and most Protestant traditions take a different position. The Lambeth Conference 1930 was a turning point: for the first time, Anglican bishops accepted that contraception could be morally acceptable within a faithful marriage if used responsibly. Most Anglican, Methodist and other Protestant churches today leave the decision about contraception to couples, trusting their moral discernment.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae (1968) by Pope Paul VI rejected artificial contraception, teaching that every act of sex must remain open to new life. CCC 2362–2363 affirms the goodness of sexual love within marriage, united with its procreative purpose. These two sources are the key Catholic authorities on this topic.

Judaism

Jewish teaching on sex and contraception varies significantly between Orthodox and Reform (Progressive) communities. In Orthodox Judaism, the first commandment in the Torah is to “be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28), meaning that openness to children is a high religious duty. However, the Talmud and rabbinic authorities have historically permitted contraception for women in certain circumstances — for example, where pregnancy would pose a health risk. The form of contraception matters: methods that do not destroy male seed are generally more acceptable than those that do in traditional halachic reasoning. Reform and Progressive Judaism generally leaves contraceptive decisions to individuals, supporting modern medical practice and reproductive autonomy.

On divorce, the Torah (Deuteronomy 24:1–4) makes provision for a man to give his wife a bill of divorce (get). In Orthodox Judaism, a religious divorce requires the husband to issue the get; a woman cannot unilaterally obtain one. This has created a significant social problem where some husbands refuse to issue the get, leaving women as agunot (chained women) — unable to remarry in the eyes of Orthodox law. Reform Judaism has addressed this by granting courts the power to dissolve marriages on behalf of either party.

Islam

Islam teaches that sexual relations outside marriage are forbidden. The Qur’an (17:32) states that one should not go near unlawful sexual relations, as it is an indecent act and a wrong way. Within marriage, sexuality is regarded as a gift from God and a source of spiritual closeness as well as procreation. On contraception, many Muslim scholars permit it where there is a valid reason (spacing of children, health concerns) using the principle that temporary prevention of birth is acceptable, though permanent sterilisation is generally opposed. Majority opinion holds that abortion as contraception is not permitted.

Divorce is permitted in Islam but strongly discouraged. The Qur’an (2:229) sets out a structured process for talaq (divorce) with a waiting period (iddah) to allow for reconciliation. The Qur’an (4:35) encourages arbitration by family members before divorce is finalised. Women can seek divorce through a legal process (khul’). Remarriage after divorce is permitted.

In Hindu teaching, sex within the context of the householder (grihastha) stage of life fulfils a legitimate purpose as part of dharmic duty. The Bhagavata Purana (5.5.8) suggests that sex motivated solely by bodily pleasure, divorced from its role in maintaining righteous family life, leads to negative consequences in terms of karma. However, many contemporary Hindu communities in Britain take a more flexible view, with traditional and modern perspectives coexisting. Contraception is not categorically prohibited; the intention behind family planning matters. Arranged marriage is still common, and divorce, while not ideal, is recognised as necessary in some cases. Views on same-sex relationships differ: traditional dharmic frameworks associate marriage with the householder ashrama designed for the continuation of family, while many Hindu communities in Britain take a more open position.

Sikhism

The Guru Granth Sahib (335) contains teachings about the spiritual dimension of human relationships, emphasising that the body is sacred and that life should be lived in accordance with God’s will (hukam). Sikhism does not have a formal prohibition on contraception and generally leaves such decisions to couples. Sex within marriage is regarded as a positive part of human life; sex outside marriage is discouraged as it can lead to attachment and suffering. On divorce, the Rehat Maryada (Sikh code of conduct, Chapter 11, Article 18) does not explicitly prohibit it but emphasises that marriage is a lifelong commitment. Guru Granth Sahib 274 stresses the importance of faithfulness in marriage.

Buddhism

The Third Precept in Buddhism is to refrain from sexual misconduct. In traditional Theravada interpretation, this means avoiding adultery, sex with those who are “already taken,” and relationships based on exploitation or harm. It does not necessarily mean sex outside marriage is always wrong, since Buddhism does not require a formal marriage ceremony — what matters is whether the relationship causes harm. Monks and nuns in the Theravada tradition are celibate; in the Zen tradition, monks may marry. The Triratna Buddhist Community (formerly the Friends of the Western Buddhist Order) takes an inclusive approach, focusing on whether a relationship is ethical and free from exploitation rather than on its formal structure. On contraception, there is no Buddhist prohibition — responsible family planning is generally accepted.

Key Fact

The Third Precept prohibits sexual misconduct. The Triratna Buddhist Community takes an inclusive approach, distinguishing between ethical and unethical relationships based on the presence or absence of harm and exploitation — not on whether the couple are formally married.

Non-Religious Perspectives

Humanists support individual autonomy in sexual ethics, arguing that consenting adults have the right to make their own decisions about relationships and contraception. They strongly support access to contraception as a matter of reproductive health and human rights. On divorce, Humanists argue that unhappy or harmful marriages should be dissoluble, and that the quality of a relationship matters more than its legal status. They typically oppose religious restrictions on contraception or divorce that they consider harmful to individuals, particularly women.

Most traditions prohibit adultery. The Ten Commandments include “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14), and all six traditions regard sexual faithfulness within marriage as important. On divorce and remarriage, responses differ significantly. Catholic Christianity does not permit divorce (only annulment in exceptional cases where the marriage was invalid from the start). Most Protestant churches permit divorce in cases of adultery or irretrievable breakdown, citing Matthew 19:8–9 (Jesus acknowledging that Moses permitted divorce “because of the hardness of your hearts”). Mark 10:9 records Jesus saying “what God has joined together, let no one separate.” Islam permits divorce through talaq (Qur’an 2:229) and remarriage. Judaism requires a get for a valid Orthodox divorce. Buddhism and Sikhism do not prohibit divorce, though both regard marriage as a serious commitment not to be ended lightly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On contraception questions, examiners report that the strongest answers specifically cite Humanae Vitae (1968, Pope Paul VI) and explain what it teaches — not just that “Catholics are against contraception.” For Protestant views, reference the Lambeth Conference 1930 as the moment Anglican teaching shifted. Always explain what the source teaches and why it leads to the position described. For evaluation questions on sexual ethics, include the Humanist perspective alongside religious views, as many mark schemes specifically reward this.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic Natural Law (Aquinas) holds that sex must always be open to new life; Humanae Vitae (1968, Pope Paul VI) rejects artificial contraception on these grounds; CCC 2362–2363 affirms sexual love within marriage as holy. Most Protestant traditions accept contraception after the Lambeth Conference 1930.
  • Islam permits contraception for valid reasons and allows divorce through talaq with a waiting period; Judaism requires the get for an Orthodox divorce and varies on contraception between Orthodox and Reform communities.
  • Buddhism’s Third Precept prohibits sexual misconduct rather than sex outside marriage per se; the Triratna community focuses on whether a relationship is ethical and free from harm rather than on formal marital status.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why some religious traditions oppose the use of artificial contraception.

[2 marks]

Developing: Two views without genuine contrast.
Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious attitudes towards sexual ethics are outdated and harmful.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Restrictions on contraception (Humanae Vitae) are criticised for contributing to population pressure and limiting women's reproductive autonomy.
• The Jewish get system has been criticised for leaving some women unable to remarry in Orthodox law.
• Some Islamic and traditional Christian views on gender roles are seen by critics as limiting women's equality.
• Humanists argue individuals should have autonomy over their own sexual and reproductive lives.

Arguments against:
• Catholic Natural Law provides a coherent ethical framework grounding sex in human nature and dignity, not arbitrary rules.
• Religious teachings on fidelity and commitment protect individuals and families from the harms of casual or exploitative relationships.
• Many religious traditions have engaged seriously with changing social contexts — e.g. Lambeth 1930 (Anglican contraception), Reform Judaism on divorce, Triratna on same-sex relationships.
• Many believers find religious sexual ethics liberating rather than restrictive, providing a framework of meaning within which relationships flourish.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced evaluation; multiple traditions engaged; Humanist view included; clear justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with references; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument; limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

lessons.title: Same-Sex Relationships
lessons.description: How different religious traditions interpret scripture to respond to same-sex relationships.
lessons.content_html:
Same-Sex Relationships in the Modern World

In 2013, the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 came into force in March 2014, allowing same-sex couples to marry in England and Wales. Civil partnerships had already been available since 2005. These legal changes have prompted significant debate within religious communities about whether such relationships align with their teachings. Different traditions — and different groups within each tradition — have reached different conclusions, often based on how they interpret the same scriptural texts.

Key Fact

The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 came into force in March 2014, legalising same-sex marriage. Civil partnerships had been available since 2005. Religious communities vary widely in how they respond to these legal changes.

Christianity

Christianity does not hold a single view on same-sex relationships. Attitudes range from full acceptance to traditional opposition, often shaped by how believers interpret specific biblical passages. The texts most frequently cited in opposition include Leviticus 20:13 and 1 Timothy 1:8–10. Those who take a traditionalist approach argue these verses clearly prohibit same-sex sexual activity. Those who take a more contextual approach argue these passages addressed specific practices in ancient cultures and cannot simply be applied to committed, loving relationships today.

The Catholic Church teaches, in Catechism paragraphs 2357–2359, that same-sex attraction is not sinful in itself, but that same-sex sexual activity is contrary to natural law. The Church calls gay and lesbian people to live chastely and to be treated with respect and compassion, while maintaining that marriage is between a man and a woman. Catholic teaching therefore opposes same-sex marriage.

Anglican views are more diverse. The Church of England has not authorised same-sex marriage ceremonies, though it has permitted prayers of blessing for same-sex couples. Some Anglican dioceses and individual clergy are more affirming than official guidance, creating significant internal debate. By contrast, Quakers in Britain have affirmed same-sex marriage since 2009 and perform same-sex ceremonies in their meeting houses, arguing that love between two people reflects the divine light present in every person.

Leviticus 20:13 is part of the Holiness Code in the Hebrew Bible and has historically been read by many Christians as a prohibition on male same-sex intercourse. Critics of this application note that the same code forbids many things modern Christians do not observe, such as eating shellfish, and argue consistency requires understanding the text in its ancient context.

1 Timothy 1:8–10 lists various behaviours the writer regards as contrary to sound teaching. Traditionalists include same-sex activity within this list. Progressive scholars dispute the translation of the Greek terms used and argue the passage targets exploitative or violent behaviour rather than consensual same-sex relationships.

The creation account in Genesis 1:27 states that God created human beings “male and female,” which some Christians take as establishing heterosexual partnership as the norm. Others note that Genesis does not explicitly discuss same-sex relationships at all, and that Galatians 3:28 — which declares there is “neither male nor female” in Christ — points toward an inclusive vision of humanity.

Judaism

Jewish attitudes divide significantly along Orthodox and Reform lines. Orthodox Judaism maintains that same-sex sexual activity is prohibited by Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which form part of the Torah’s Holiness Code. Orthodox communities do not recognise or perform same-sex marriages, though they call for respectful treatment of gay and lesbian individuals.

Reform Judaism, by contrast, has moved to full affirmation of same-sex relationships. Liberal and Reform synagogues in Britain perform same-sex commitment ceremonies and, following the Marriage Act, same-sex marriages. The movement grounds this in the principle of human dignity (kavod ha-beriyot) and the commandment to love one’s neighbour. This represents a genuine diversity of interpretation within a single religious tradition.

Islam

Mainstream Islamic scholarship holds that same-sex sexual activity is prohibited. This position draws on Qur’an 7:80–81, which refers to the people of Lut (Lot) and describes their practice as a transgression. Muslim scholars across different schools of jurisprudence have generally agreed that sexual relationships are intended for marriage between a man and a woman, and that this reflects the natural order as God designed it. The majority of Muslim communities in Britain oppose same-sex marriage, though individual Muslims hold a range of personal views. Islam teaches that people experiencing same-sex attraction should be treated with dignity while being encouraged to live according to Islamic law.

Hinduism

Traditional Hindu teaching has linked sexual activity closely to the householder ashrama, where the purpose of sexual relations is connected to procreation and the continuation of family lineage, as part of one’s dharma. Under this framework, same-sex relationships may be seen as conflicting with the dharma of the householder. However, views within Hinduism are diverse. Hinduism has no single central authority, and there are ancient texts, art, and temple sculptures that depict same-sex intimacy without condemnation. Many Hindus in Britain take a more accepting view of same-sex relationships, and the Hindu Council UK has acknowledged diverse opinions within the community.

Sikhism

The Lavan, the four sacred stanzas recited during the Sikh marriage ceremony, describes the progressive union of a man and a woman with the divine. The Sikh Rehat Maryada (code of conduct) defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and most Sikh religious authorities oppose same-sex marriage. Nine of the ten Gurus were married to women, and marriage is seen as a spiritual journey that the Lavan describes in gendered terms. As with other traditions, however, individual Sikhs hold a range of views, and some Sikh voices call for greater inclusion of LGBTQ+ members in the community.

Key Fact

Sikh teaching draws on the Lavan (the four marriage stanzas) to understand marriage as between a man and a woman. The Catholic Catechism (2357–2359) distinguishes between same-sex attraction (not sinful) and same-sex sexual activity (contrary to natural law).

Buddhism

Buddhism has no single official teaching on same-sex relationships. The Third Precept calls Buddhists to refrain from sexual misconduct, but what counts as misconduct is interpreted differently across traditions. Some Theravada teachers argue that the Third Precept implies sexual activity should be within a committed, procreative context; others argue it is about the harm caused by an action rather than the gender of the parties. The Triratna Buddhist Community (formerly the Friends of the Western Buddhist Order) has been broadly affirming of LGBTQ+ members. There is no pan-Buddhist consensus, and the lack of an official position reflects Buddhism’s decentralised nature.

Humanists UK fully supports same-sex relationships and conducts humanist same-sex ceremonies. Humanist ethics begin with the wellbeing of persons and the principle of consent rather than with religious authority. From a humanist standpoint, a loving, committed same-sex relationship is as morally equivalent to a heterosexual relationship, because what matters is the quality of the relationship — honesty, care, and mutual respect — not the genders of the people involved. Humanists argue that laws and social norms should reflect evidence about human flourishing rather than ancient religious texts.

Evaluating the Debate

The debate over same-sex relationships within and between religious traditions illustrates a broader question: how should ancient scriptural texts be applied in a contemporary legal and social context? Conservative voices argue that scripture provides timeless moral guidance and that reinterpreting it to suit modern values undermines its authority. Progressive voices argue that faithfulness to the spirit of a tradition — love, compassion, human dignity — sometimes requires updating its specific applications. Students should be able to present both positions with supporting evidence and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 15-mark evaluation questions on same-sex relationships, you must present both religious and non-religious perspectives. Do not just list views — explain the reasoning behind each position and quote a source of authority. For example, explaining why the Catholic Catechism distinguishes attraction from activity (natural law reasoning) is stronger than simply stating that Catholics oppose same-sex marriage. Remember to include at least one scriptural reference and reach a clear, justified personal conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 legalised same-sex marriage in England and Wales from March 2014. Religious communities hold diverse attitudes, ranging from full affirmation (Quakers, Reform Judaism, Triratna Buddhism, Humanists) to traditional opposition (Catholic, Orthodox Jewish, mainstream Islamic teaching, Sikh Rehat Maryada).
  • Key texts cited include Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 (Jewish and Christian traditionalists), 1 Timothy 1:8–10 (Christian traditionalists), and Qur’an 7:80–81 (Islamic teaching). Contextual interpreters argue these passages cannot be straightforwardly applied to modern, committed relationships.
  • Buddhism has no official position; the Third Precept is interpreted differently across traditions. Humanists ground their full acceptance in the principles of consent, wellbeing, and human dignity rather than religious authority.

lessons.title: Gender Equality and the Roles of Women and Men
lessons.description: Religious attitudes to women in worship and authority, including ordination and gender equality.
lessons.content_html:
Gender Equality: A Modern and Ancient Question

Gender equality is both a modern legal principle and an ancient religious debate. The UK Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sex in employment, education, and public services. At the same time, religious communities have debated for centuries what roles men and women should play in worship and religious authority. These debates draw on sacred texts, tradition, and changing understandings of human dignity. Different traditions — and different groups within each tradition — have reached very different conclusions.

Christianity

Christian attitudes to gender equality and women’s roles in worship are shaped by two contrasting sets of biblical passages. 1 Timothy 2:11–12 states that a woman should “learn in quietness and full submission” and not “teach or to assume authority over a man.” This passage has been used historically to restrict women from preaching and leadership. By contrast, Galatians 3:27–29 declares that in Christ “there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female” — a verse used by those who argue for full equality within the Church.

The Church of England voted to ordain women as priests in 1992 (with the first ordinations in 1994), and women bishops have been permitted since 2014. Most Anglican provinces around the world now ordain women at various levels. The Church in Wales has also ordained women as priests and bishops, reflecting the same shift in Anglican practice.

The Catholic Church, by contrast, teaches that only men can be ordained priests. Catechism paragraph 1577 states that the Church is not “authorized” to ordain women, citing Jesus’s choice of twelve male apostles and unbroken tradition. Catechism 369–373 teaches that men and women are equal in dignity and imago Dei, created as complementary rather than identical, with different but equally valued roles. Catechism paragraph 1935 states that every person possesses equal dignity before God regardless of sex.

Key Fact

The Church of England and the Church in Wales ordain women as priests and bishops. The Catholic Church reserves priestly ordination to men, citing apostolic tradition (Catechism 1577). Both affirm men and women as equal in dignity (Catechism 1935).

1 Timothy 2:11–12 is used by traditionalists to argue that women should not hold teaching authority over men in the Church. Scholars who support women’s ordination argue this passage was addressing a specific local situation in first-century Ephesus and should not be read as a universal rule.

Galatians 3:27–29 states that all who are baptised into Christ have “clothed themselves with Christ” and that “there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Egalitarian Christians argue this overrides gender-role restrictions, because baptism creates a new equality in Christ that transcends social divisions.

Judaism

As with same-sex relationships, Jewish attitudes to women’s roles divide sharply between Orthodox and Reform communities. Orthodox Judaism maintains that men and women have different but complementary roles prescribed by halakha (Jewish law). Women are exempt from many positive time-bound commandments and traditionally do not lead mixed-gender public prayer. Women cannot serve as Orthodox rabbis, and men and women sit separately in Orthodox synagogues.

Reform and Liberal Judaism ordain women as rabbis — the first female rabbi ordained in Britain was in 1975. Reform synagogues have mixed seating and women may lead all aspects of worship. The movement grounds this in the principle that the Torah’s ethical core includes full human equality, and that restrictions on women’s leadership were historically conditioned rather than divinely intended.

Islam

Islamic teaching affirms spiritual equality between men and women before God. Qur’an 4:1 refers to God creating both men and women from a single soul, affirming their common origin and dignity. Qur’an 40:40 states that whoever does good deeds, whether male or female, will enter paradise — emphasising equal spiritual accountability. However, Qur’an 2:228 notes that “men have a degree over them,” a verse that has been interpreted to support different family roles and, in traditional jurisprudence, the reservation of Friday prayer leadership to men.

In practice, women do not lead Friday prayers over mixed male-female congregations in mainstream Sunni and Shia traditions. Women may lead prayers for all-female gatherings. Some contemporary Muslim scholars argue that classical restrictions on women’s religious leadership were culturally conditioned rather than theologically required. In Britain, Muslim women hold prominent roles as scholars, educators, and community leaders, even where formal prayer leadership may be restricted.

Hinduism

Hindu texts present contrasting views on the roles of women. The Manusmriti (Law of Manu), an ancient legal text, contains passages in sections 2.67–2.68 that describe traditional roles for women and their dependence on male relatives. It also contains passages in sections 5.148–155 that further restrict women’s independence. However, sections 9.72–81 and 9.192–194 contain passages that also affirm the importance of protecting and honouring women. These tensions within a single text reflect the diversity of ancient Hindu legal thinking.

Contemporary Hinduism in Britain shows significant change. Women serve as priests in some mandirs, perform public worship, and hold leadership roles in Hindu organisations. The Ramakrishna tradition and ISKCON both include women in significant spiritual roles. Many British Hindus regard gender equality as fully consistent with Hindu principles of the divine feminine (Shakti) and the presence of Brahman in every person.

Sikhism

Sikhism formally teaches the equality of men and women. The Guru Granth Sahib, at ang (page) 473, contains the teaching that from woman man is born and that without woman there would be no creation — affirming the spiritual status of women. The ten Gurus consistently taught against discrimination on the basis of gender, caste, or religion. In principle, women may perform all religious functions in a gurdwara, including reading from the Guru Granth Sahib and leading Ardas (prayer).

In practice, some Sikh communities reflect the cultural norms of Punjab, where gender distinctions remain more marked. There is ongoing debate about women serving as granthis (readers of the scripture) in traditional gurdwaras. However, the theological position is clear: the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that the soul has no gender and that all souls are equal before God.

Key Fact

The Guru Granth Sahib (ang 473) affirms the spiritual status of women — from woman all are born, through woman the world continues. Both Sikhism and Catholicism affirm equal dignity for men and women, though they differ on whether this extends to identical roles in worship.

Buddhism

Theravada Buddhism has a traditional four-fold hierarchy: monks (bhikkhus), nuns (bhikkhunis), laymen, and laywomen. Historically, the order of fully ordained nuns died out in Theravada countries and was not revived until the modern era. Some Theravada authorities in Thailand and Sri Lanka have resisted the full reinstatement of the bhikkhuni sangha on the grounds that unbroken ordination lineage has been lost. By contrast, other Theravada teachers and most Mahayana traditions have supported full ordination for women.

In Britain, Buddhist nuns and women teachers hold prominent roles in many sanghas. Triratna ordains women on equal terms with men. The Theravada tradition at centres such as Amaravati Abbey has supported the training of women renunciants. The tension between ancient hierarchical structures and the Buddha’s own founding of the nuns’ order continues to be worked through across different traditions.

Humanists UK supports full gender equality and argues that restricting women’s roles in religious authority based on ancient texts is an example of religion being used to perpetuate inequality. From a humanist standpoint, the Equality Act 2010 reflects the rational, evidence-based principle that discrimination on grounds of sex causes harm and limits human flourishing. While religious organisations have some legal exemptions from equality legislation, humanists argue these exemptions should be narrowed rather than protected.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about gender roles in religion, be careful to distinguish between theological teaching (what a tradition officially says) and practice (what actually happens in communities). Examiners reward answers that show awareness of diversity within traditions — for example, noting that Reform and Orthodox Judaism differ sharply on women rabbis, or that Sikh theology teaches equality while some communities reflect cultural patriarchy. Always link claims to a named source of authority such as Galatians 3:27–29, Qur’an 4:1, or Guru Granth Sahib ang 473.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christian attitudes to women’s roles divide between traditions that ordain women (Church of England, Church in Wales, most Protestant churches) and those that do not (Catholic Church, some Orthodox). Key texts include 1 Timothy 2:11–12 (used to restrict) and Galatians 3:27–29 (used to affirm equality).
  • Sikhism formally teaches equal dignity for men and women (Guru Granth Sahib, ang 473); Islam affirms spiritual equality (Qur’an 4:1, 40:40) while traditional practice restricts mixed-congregation prayer leadership to men; Reform Judaism and Hinduism in Britain both show significant movement towards full equality in practice.
  • Buddhism’s Theravada tradition has historically restricted full ordination for women but this is being revisited; Humanists argue full gender equality is required by rational ethics and reflected in the Equality Act 2010.
